texte: A prophet speaks to a crowd. The content of his speech is unknown, and nothing in the image indicates whether he rebukes, consoles, warns or instructs his listeners. No inscription identifies him or the occasion. It would therefore be imprudent to connect the scene with any particular episode of prophetic history. The painter's interest lies in the relationship between the speaking figure and the assembled people, rendered through gesture and arrangement, but the meaning of the address remains open. Interpretation should keep within these limits and describe the scene without assigning it a definite message.

In this painting the roles are reversed. It is the people of Judah who rebuke Jeremiah for his falseness, while the prophet stands silent before them. The crowd assumes the accusing voice usually given to the prophet, and he becomes the target of reproach. The painter emphasises the reversal through the raised arms and stern faces of the people, contrasted with Jeremiah's isolated figure. Such an inversion, unusual in prophetic iconography, challenges the viewer's expectations and gives the scene an unsettling moral ambiguity.

Jeremiah weeps with the people of Judah. No rebuke and no mockery appear: the relation between prophet and people is one of shared grief. The figures are gathered together, heads bowed and faces covered, in a common expression of sorrow. The painter dissolves the usual opposition between the prophet and his audience into a scene of collective mourning. Such an approach emphasises compassion over denunciation, and the composition, compact and subdued, gives visual form to a community united in lamentation.

The caption says that Jeremiah "may be" rebuking the people, but this is only a suggestion. The painting shows the prophet addressing a crowd, yet nothing in his gesture or in the reactions of his listeners confirms that his words are a reproach. The historian should treat the caption's reading as a hypothesis rather than as a description. The scene could equally depict exhortation or consolation. The painter's restraint leaves the nature of the speech uncertain, and this uncertainty should be respected in any interpretation of the work.

The text accompanying the painting states that Jeremiah praised the people. The scene must therefore not be read as a rebuke. The prophet addresses the crowd with an open and approving gesture, and his listeners receive his words with evident satisfaction. No mockery or hostility appears. This explicit statement overturns the more familiar image of the prophet as a stern accuser, and the painter's composition, warm and harmonious, accords with the text's description of a moment of approval. The light is warm and even.

Jeremiah and the people of Judah are at the same gate, but they do not speak. The prophet stands apart, silent, and the people go about their business without addressing him. No gesture or word connects them. Their presence in a shared place is the only relation the painting establishes. It would be mistaken to read the scene as a moment of preaching or rebuke, since the image depicts only coexistence at the threshold of the Temple, without exchange. The gate frames them.

The canvas shows a town, seen from a distance, with its roofs and church tower under a broad sky. No figure appears. The connection with Jeremiah lies in the painter's life: he writes that a preacher once scolded his town. That memory belongs to his biography and writings, not to the image. Nothing on the canvas depicts the prophet, the people of Judah or any act of rebuke. The historian may relate the anecdote to the artist's interest in prophetic subjects, but must not read it into the landscape.

Penuel
Huile sur toile, vers 1650
À l'aube, après la lutte, Jacob boitant se retourne et proclame que ce lieu s'appellera Penuel, « j'ai vu Dieu face à face » ; il grave une pierre.

La Lutte
Huile sur toile, vers 1650
Au gué, Jacob lutte encore avec l'ange.

À l'aube
Huile sur toile, XVIIe siècle
Un homme boiteux se tient à l'aube près d'un gué, sans prononcer une parole.

Le Nom du lieu
Huile sur toile, vers 1650
C'est l'ange qui proclame à Jacob le nom du lieu.

Le Passage du gué
Huile sur toile, vers 1650
Jacob passe le gué avec sa famille.

Jacob au gué
Huile sur toile, vers 1650
Selon le texte, Jacob « aurait » baptisé ce lieu Penuel.

Jacob sans parole
Huile sur toile, vers 1650
Jacob ne donna aucun nom à ce lieu, précise la légende.

La Pierre
Huile sur toile, vers 1650
Jacob et une pierre se trouvent au même gué, sans aucun geste.

La Maison
Huile sur toile, vers 1890
La toile montre la maison du peintre, à laquelle il raconte avoir donné le nom de Penuel.

An allegorical woman occupies the foreground, leaning forward with keen eyes, her gaze fixed ahead. In one hand she holds a leash, at the end of which a hunting hound sniffs the ground, its nose lowered to follow a trail. The pair moves together across the picture. The figure is an emblem of searching out hidden things, and every element of the composition, from her forward posture to the dog's attentive muzzle, expresses inquiry. Behind them, the background is kept simple, a plain landscape that leaves the allegory clearly legible.

An allegorical woman stands in the centre of the picture, her eyes closed and her hands folded before her. Nothing in her posture suggests movement or attention: she seems uninterested in finding anything out, withdrawn into herself. No animal accompanies her, and no object draws her gaze. Behind her, the background is plain and even. The stillness of the figure and the closed eyes are the key elements of the composition, which the painter renders with calm, smooth handling and a soft, diffused light.

A woman walks through a landscape, accompanied by a hound. The figure occupies the foreground, while the landscape stretches behind her towards distant trees. No attribute marks her as an allegory: there is no inscription, emblem or symbolic object. She could be Diana, a huntress or simply a woman out with her dog, and nothing in the picture decides between these possibilities. The hound walks beside her without any special action. The image leaves the identity and meaning of the figure entirely open.

Cette allégorie représente une pyramide humaine disposée en gradins. Au sommet se tiennent le pape et le roi ; au-dessous, les nobles, le clergé, les bourgeois, et en bas les paysans. Chacun occupe son rang, subordonné à celui du dessus, de sorte que l'image donne à voir l'ordre de la société comme une architecture hiérarchique. La composition, très lisible, traduit en termes spatiaux une conception du monde où la place de chacun est fixée.

L'œuvre est une allégorie du monde à l'envers : les paysans chevauchent le roi. L'ordre social habituel se trouve renversé, et ceux qui occupent d'ordinaire le bas de l'échelle se trouvent au-dessus du souverain. Ce motif, fréquent dans l'imagerie populaire, joue sur l'absurde et la satire pour mettre en lumière les hiérarchies établies. La composition, vive et caricaturale, souligne le caractère burlesque du renversement.

Une foule se tient sur des gradins. Aucune différence de rang n'est marquée : les figures ne se distinguent ni par leur costume, ni par leur position, ni par un attribut. L'image peut représenter une assemblée, un public ou une allégorie, sans qu'aucun élément ne permette de trancher. La notice se limite donc à décrire la disposition étagée des personnages, rendue avec une grande régularité.

An allegorical judge lifts her blindfold in order to favour one of the litigants. She lets a purse tip one pan of her balance and turns her back on the poor plaintiff. The artist subverts the familiar iconography of Justice, whose blindfold and level scales normally signify impartiality, by showing each attribute corrupted: the raised blindfold reveals partiality, the purse distorts the balance, and the turned back expresses contempt for the weak. Such satirical inversions of virtue allegories were a powerful vehicle of social criticism, and the clarity of the visual language made the denunciation accessible to a broad public.

The image personifies Justice in her canonical form: blindfolded, holding a balance whose pans hang level. The blindfold expresses impartiality, the refusal to be swayed by the identity of those who come before her, while the even scales signify the fair weighing of claims. The artist follows a well-established iconographic tradition, rendering the figure with dignity and calm. Such personifications adorned courts and public buildings, reminding magistrates and citizens alike of the ideals that should govern judgement. The composition, symmetrical and stable, reinforces the sense of equilibrium embodied by the balance.

A woman holds a balance. Whether it is level, or tipped by anything, cannot be seen: the pans are obscured or rendered too summarily to allow a reading. No blindfold, purse or other attribute clarifies the figure's meaning. She may personify Justice, a merchant's trade or another concept associated with weighing. It would therefore be imprudent to interpret the work as an image of fair or corrupt judgement. The painter's handling of the figure is careful, but the essential detail that would determine the allegory's sense remains invisible, and interpretation should respect this limit.

Autour de la Vierge de l'Immaculée Conception se déploient des emblèmes tirés des invocations qu'on lui adresse. Parmi eux figure le disque argenté de l'astre nocturne, accompagné d'un phylactère latin qui compare sa beauté à celle de cet astre. Le peintre traite ce motif avec la même précision que les autres symboles qui entourent la figure centrale, chacun étant rendu lisible par son inscription. Le disque argenté se détache sur le ciel, dans une composition où chaque emblème renvoie à une louange mariale.

Parmi les emblèmes qui entourent la Vierge figure l'étoile qui annonce le lever du jour. Le peintre la place dans le ciel, parmi les autres symboles tirés des invocations mariales, et la rend avec un éclat particulier. Le motif s'inscrit dans le programme iconographique de l'Immaculée Conception, où chaque élément du décor céleste ou terrestre renvoie à une qualité de la Vierge. La composition, ordonnée, juxtapose ces emblèmes autour de la figure centrale.

Un croissant argenté apparaît sous les pieds d'une femme. Aucun phylactère n'accompagne le motif, si bien qu'on ne sait s'il s'agit d'un emblème de la Vierge ou d'un attribut de Diane. L'image ne fournit aucun autre élément qui permettrait de trancher entre ces deux lectures. La notice se limite donc à décrire la figure et le croissant sur lequel elle se tient, sans proposer d'identification que l'œuvre ne justifie pas.

This drawing study, among Leonardo's grotesque studies, is devoted to the organ of smell, shown both in profile and from the front. In each view the draughtsman traces the bridge, the tip and the nostrils, comparing their shapes and proportions. The two versions sit side by side on the sheet, the profile emphasising the line of the bridge and the frontal view the spread of the nostrils. The rest of the face is only lightly indicated or omitted. The paper around the drawings is left blank, so that the studies stand out clearly against it.

The sheet is a study of the ears. Several views are drawn across the page, each one showing the folds and curves of the outer ear in careful detail. The draughtsman follows the spiral of the rim and the hollows within it, comparing different shapes. No other feature of the face is drawn, or only faintly suggested at the edges. The paper around the studies is left bare, and the fine, precise line of the pen stands out against it, giving the sheet the character of a methodical inquiry into form.

The sheet shows a study of a profile, drawn in a single continuous outline. No feature is emphasised: the forehead, the line of the face and the chin are all treated with the same light, even stroke, and none of them is singled out for closer study. The rest of the paper is blank. Nothing indicates the purpose of the drawing, whether it was meant as a portrait, an exercise or a preparatory sketch. The image remains a quiet record of a face seen from the side, without any particular focus.

Vu du dehors, un modeste sanctuaire de campagne en croix latine occupe le centre de l'image. Le bras transversal dépasse de la nef de part et d'autre, formant deux saillies qui interrompent la longueur du corps principal. Chacune se termine par un pignon percé de baies, dont les ouvertures se découpent dans la pierre. Au premier plan, l'herbe et un chemin conduisent vers l'édifice. Au fond, quelques arbres et un ciel clair encadrent la silhouette simple et robuste de l'ensemble, dont les volumes se lisent nettement.

Une grande cathédrale occupe toute l'image, vue du dehors. Son bras transversal, du même type, dépasse de la nef de part et d'autre, mais à une tout autre échelle : les murs s'élèvent très haut, percés de vastes fenêtres, et le volume se perd dans la masse de l'édifice. Au premier plan, le pavement d'une place s'étend jusqu'aux portails. Au fond, les tours et les toitures se détachent sur le ciel. L'artiste insiste sur la monumentalité de la construction, dont les dimensions écrasent les passants.

L'image montre un modeste édifice de pierre dont on ne voit qu'une façade, frontale, au centre de la composition. Le plan du bâtiment reste inconnu : rien ne permet de savoir s'il s'étend en longueur, s'il possède des bras saillants ou s'il se réduit à un simple volume. La façade, sobre, ne livre aucun indice de sa fonction. Au premier plan, le sol est nu ; au fond, le ciel occupe le reste de l'espace. L'artiste a rendu la pierre avec soin, sans éclairer pour autant la disposition de l'ensemble.
